passage:
In the library period, a video of Siddharth tripping on the stage steps was going round the class. Comments piled up under it. Rehana held her phone under the desk. Ayaan had written “Gold medal for falling,” and others added laughing lines. She typed, “Nice landing champ,” and pressed send. Thirty likes in a minute. It felt like tossing a coin into a fountain; nobody could really be hurt. Zoya, beside her, put her phone away and said nothing.

Next morning Siddharth sat at the back with his hood up. The comments were all still there, fifty of them. Rehana read her own line as if Siddharth were reading it, and her stomach dropped. She deleted it and went to sit beside him.

qa.q: What did Rehana type under the video?
qa.a: Rehana typed, “Nice landing champ.”

qa.q: Why did the comment feel harmless to Rehana at first?
qa.a: Many others were doing the same, so it felt like tossing a coin into a fountain, and nobody seemed really hurt.

qa.q: What choice did Rehana make the next morning?
qa.a: Rehana deleted the comment and went to sit beside Siddharth.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have felt, sitting at the back with the hood up while the comments stayed?
qa.a: Siddharth probably felt exposed and ashamed, knowing every one of the fifty comments could be read.

grounding: A teenager adds a mocking comment to a viral video because many others are doing so, then realises the target sees every word.

passage:
Dear Himani,

I'm writing because I'm too ashamed to say this in class. On Tuesday the video of you slipping at the sports meet was all over our class group. Everyone was posting jokes, even Ritu and Deepak. Only Kabir said, “Stop it,” and we ignored him. I wrote one too: “Ground record for the fastest slide.” I told myself it was just a joke and would get lost among so many.

Then on Wednesday I saw you at the gate, checking your phone with your face closed, and I realised you had read every single one.

I deleted mine. This morning I told Mr. Rao what I did. He sat the whole group down at lunch and had the video taken down. I'm sorry, Himani.

Yash

qa.q: What joke did Yash write under the video?
qa.a: Yash wrote, “Ground record for the fastest slide.”

qa.q: Why did Yash think Himani would never see the joke?
qa.a: Yash assumed it was just a joke that would get lost among so many comments.

qa.q: What did Yash do after realising Himani had read every comment?
qa.a: Yash deleted the joke and told Mr. Rao what had been done.

qa.q: What might Himani have felt at the gate, checking a phone with a closed face?
qa.a: Himani probably felt exposed and hurt, reading each comment alone.

grounding: A teenager who added a mocking comment to a viral video writes to the target after seeing that every word was read.

subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
In her bedroom in Nairobi, Esther scrolled through the video everyone was sharing: a girl from another school, Nkechi, slipping on stage at a talent show and landing on her back mid-song. It had a hundred thousand views.
The comments were endless. “Gravity 1, her 0.” “Who let her on stage?”
Esther laughed and typed, “She should stick to singing in the shower,” with a laughing face. Her comment got forty likes in a minute. It felt like nothing. Just one more voice.
Later, scrolling again, she saw a reply from Nkechi's own account under all of them: “I can read these, you know.”
Esther looked at her own comment for a long time. Then she deleted it, though she knew Nkechi had already seen it.

qa.q: How many views did the video have?
qa.a: It had a hundred thousand views.

qa.q: How did Esther feel when she first posted the comment?
qa.a: She felt detached and amused, as if it was nothing, just one more voice among many.

qa.q: What could Esther do now beyond deleting the comment?
qa.a: She could send Nkechi a private apology and choose not to add to pile-ons in future.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt reading every comment?
qa.a: She was probably humiliated and hurt, seeing strangers mock her after a painful fall.

grounding: Shows a teenager adding a mocking comment to a viral post because many others did, feeling it harmless until the target replies.

passage:
In the boys' hostel, a clip of Tarun singing off-key at the hostel night was going round the student page. The comments were brutal and funny.
Tenzin, in his room, laughed out loud. He had a spare account with no name and no photo. He typed, “Somebody call a vet, a cat is dying,” and hit post. Within an hour it was the top comment.
He felt nothing much. There were three hundred comments. His was just one.
At dinner in the mess, Tarun sat alone at the end of the table, eating fast, not looking at anyone. Somebody behind Tenzin whispered, “Vet! Vet!” and a few boys laughed. Tarun's ears went red.
Tenzin stopped chewing. His comment was sitting at the table with them.

qa.q: What did Tenzin's comment say?
qa.a: It said, "Somebody call a vet, a cat is dying."

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when he posted the comment?
qa.a: He felt amused and careless, as if one comment among three hundred didn't matter.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do after dinner?
qa.a: He could delete the comment, apologise to Tarun, and stop others repeating the "vet" joke.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when the boys whispered "Vet!"?
qa.a: Tarun likely felt humiliated and alone, ears going red as the online joke followed him into the mess.

grounding: Shows a teenager adding an anonymous mocking comment to a viral clip, feeling it harmless, until he sees the target hurt in person.

passage:
Dear Lakshmi,
You don't know me. I'm Siddharth, from the school across the road. Last week your poster for the science fair went viral because of the spelling mistake, and I commented, “Scinece fair lol, go back to Class 2.”
When I wrote it, there were already five hundred comments. It felt like throwing a stone into the sea. It didn't feel like anything.
Then my cousin showed me your post saying you'd stopped going to the fair committee meetings. I read all the comments again, from your side. Every single one was a stone, and they all landed on you.
I've deleted mine. I'm sorry. If you're ever at the fair, I'd like to see your project.
Siddharth

qa.q: What did Siddharth's comment say?
qa.a: Siddharth commented, "Scinece fair lol, go back to Class 2."

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when writing the comment, compared to later?
qa.a: At first Siddharth felt detached, like throwing a stone into the sea, but later ashamed on seeing it from Lakshmi's side.

qa.q: What makes Siddharth's letter a good repair?
qa.a: It admits exactly what was written, deletes it, apologises, and shows real interest in Lakshmi's project.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Lakshmi might feel surprised and a bit comforted that one person saw the hurt and cared enough to apologise.

grounding: A teenager writes to apologise for adding a mocking comment to a viral post, once the writer realises the target saw every word.

subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
Okay, I'll say it, since this podcast is about online stuff. I'm Kamal, I'm fifteen, and last month I was part of a pile-on.
A boy from another school, Wasim, posted a dance video. His foot slipped at the end. Someone reposted it with a laughing caption, and it blew up. Two thousand comments. Everyone was writing stuff like "bro fell harder than my marks." I thought it was funny. I added one: "bro dances like a folding chair." It got forty likes. I felt clever the whole evening. With two thousand people, one more comment didn't feel like anything.
A week later, a friend of a friend said Wasim had stopped coming to school. That's when it hit me. He'd read every single one. Including mine.
I deleted it that night and told my class teacher, who said she'd contact his school's counsellor the next morning. I still don't know if that's enough.

qa.q: How many comments did the reposted video get?
qa.a: Two thousand comments.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel after posting the comment, and then a week later?
qa.a: Kamal felt clever and pleased with the forty likes, then guilty and shaken on hearing Wasim had stopped coming to school.

qa.q: What could Kamal do besides deleting the comment?
qa.a: Kamal could send Wasim a short private apology and stay out of future pile-ons, remembering the target reads every word.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Wasim to read the comments?
qa.a: Wasim was probably humiliated and hurt, with two thousand strangers mocking one slip, so staying home felt safer.

grounding: Shows a teenager adding a mocking comment to a viral post because many others were, feeling it harmless until realising the target read every word.
